title: US bans some Canadian dairy and alcohol as the tariff war escalates
deck: Washington turned 50% tariffs on certain Canadian dairy and alcohol products into import bans, Canada hit back dollar for dollar, and the fight now sits inside the US midterms, the USMCA review and the aftermath of Alberta's 19 October vote to stay in Canada.

card.headline: The US has moved from tariffs to bans on certain Canadian dairy and alcohol products, and Canada is retaliating in kind

keyNumber.label: US Section 338 tariff on about $20bn of Canadian goods, in force since 22 August; certain alcohol and dairy products now banned

forYou.line: Certain Canadian alcohol and dairy products are banned, and furniture, clothing, ATVs and other listed goods face 50% duties whatever their USMCA origin. Check each tariff line, because goods under Section 232 are treated separately.
Canada's counter-tariffs cover US steel, dairy, appliances and farm equipment. Expect lost price competitiveness and possible order shifts.
Canadian-origin products are being removed from GSA Multiple Award Schedules. Check whether any Canadian-made items sit in your federal catalogue.
Watch the 3 November US midterms and the 12 January 2027 USMCA comment deadline. Both could move the odds of a deal.
US shoppers may see higher prices for cheese, furniture and other covered Canadian goods. Canadians may see fewer US goods on shelves and higher prices for them.

effects.text: Certain Canadian alcohol and dairy products are barred from the US market from 29 September
50% Section 338 duties hit furniture, clothing and ATVs, and apply regardless of USMCA origin
Canada's counter-tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances and farm equipment have applied since 8 September
Canadian-origin products removed from GSA federal procurement schedules
Higher US shelf prices for cheese, furniture and other covered Canadian goods, weeks before the 3 November vote
Canadian dairy and winery producers must find other buyers or cut output
US appliance, steel and farm-equipment makers lose price competitiveness in Canada
Importers rewrite contracts and reroute sourcing as Section 338 duties sit alongside Section 232 and other tariffs
Canada courts the EU and other partners, making EU CBAM and EUDR compliance a live export issue
Alberta voted on 19 October, by about 77%, to stay in Canada, but grievances about Ottawa and market access remain
USMCA, now on yearly reviews, becomes a bargaining chip, with dairy among the US demands
Long-run investment decisions in Canada and the US factor in permanent tariff risk

whatHappened: President Trump proclaimed 50% tariffs under Section 338 on 20 July. Talks collapsed on 21 August and the tariffs took effect on 22 August, covering about $20 billion of Canadian goods, including wine, furniture, dairy, cement and clothing.

Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed on 22 August to match the US tariffs dollar for dollar. His counter-tariffs, in force from 8 September, cover US steel, dairy, appliances and farm equipment among other goods. The White House puts them at about $20 billion of US exports. Covington, a law firm, reports more than 600 product categories and $27.6 billion of US goods, with a C$7.5 billion support package for Canadian firms.

On 8 September President Trump signed five proclamations. They turn the 50% duties on certain Canadian alcohol and dairy products into import bans from 29 September, remove rock salt and cement from the tariff list and add ATVs and more dairy products from 15 September, and order Canadian-origin products off GSA Multiple Award Schedules.

Section 338 duties apply regardless of USMCA origin. The White House says they apply in addition to Section 232 tariffs, while legal summaries of the July proclamations say goods already under Section 232, such as steel, aluminium, vehicles and certain wood products, are excluded from them.
whyItMatters: The US takes nearly 70% of Canada's exports, and the goods first hit were about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US. Bans and 50% duties are a heavier tool than the earlier tariffs.

Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 lets a president impose duties of up to 50% on countries that discriminate against US commerce, and to ban imports if the discrimination continues. This is the first time it has ever been used to impose tariffs, and a lawsuit challenging the duties was reported on 20 October.

The dispute is one confrontation with the USMCA review. The US declined on 1 July to extend the pact for 16 years, so it must now be reviewed every year, and US demands include wider access for US dairy.
It lands weeks before US midterms dominated by living costs, and just after Alberta voted on 19 October, by about 77%, to stay in Canada.

winners.why: Some competing Canadian products are barred, and Canadian retaliation on US dairy is only one front in their business.
It is courting a bilateral deal and has pledged to buy more American goods. Canada's exclusion may raise its relative value to Washington.
Canada is courting them to diversify away from the US, which may open market share for them.

losers.who: Canadian dairy farmers, wineries and distillers
losers.why: They lose access to the US market for banned products, and not only through higher duties.

losers.who: Canadian furniture, clothing and other listed exporters
losers.why: They face a 50% tariff that applies even to USMCA-origin goods.
Prices for cheese, furniture and other covered goods are likely to rise, and sourcing is disrupted.

losers.who: US steel, appliance and farm-equipment makers
losers.why: They are hit by Canada's counter-tariffs.

whatsNext: 3 November: US midterm elections. Cost of living is the dominant issue.
Pending: a lawsuit challenging the Section 338 duties, reported on 20 October.
30 December: the EU Deforestation Regulation starts to apply to large and medium operators, relevant to Canadian exporters diversifying to Europe.
12 January 2027: written comments and hearing requests due in the USTR's 2027 USMCA review.
1 February 2027: EU CBAM certificate sales open.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what do you think is the most likely path through the end of 2026?
options: Full deal and removal of the bans
Prolonged standoff with the bans and counter-tariffs in place
Court ruling strikes down Section 338 duties
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 50%, is a prolonged standoff. Both sides have locked in measures, the USMCA review runs on yearly cycles, and the US midterms reduce the incentive to concede before 3 November. This is author judgement.

timeline.title: Iran war begins
timeline.detail: Fuel and grocery price rises since then are the dominant US midterm issue and shape the political cost of tariffs.

timeline.title: US declines to extend USMCA by 16 years
timeline.detail: Under Article 34.7 the pact now runs only to 1 July 2036 and must be reviewed every year.

timeline.title: Trump proclaims 50% Section 338 tariffs
timeline.detail: Three proclamations target Canadian measures on alcohol, dairy and motor vehicles. The start date was later set for 22 August.

timeline.title: Talks collapse; 50% Section 338 tariffs take effect
timeline.detail: Talks broke down late on 21 August. The duties cover about $20bn of Canadian goods, including wine, furniture, dairy, cement and clothing.

timeline.title: Canada vows retaliation
timeline.detail: Carney says Canada will match the new US tariffs dollar for dollar from 8 September.

timeline.title: Canada sets out its counter-tariffs
timeline.detail: More than 600 product categories at 15%, 25% or 50%, which Covington puts at $27.6bn of US goods, plus a C$7.5bn support package.

timeline.title: Canadian counter-tariffs take effect; Trump signs five proclamations
timeline.detail: Canada's duties, which the White House puts at about $20bn of US exports including steel, dairy and farm equipment, apply. Trump turns the 50% duties on certain Canadian alcohol and dairy products into bans from 29 September and orders Canadian-origin products off GSA schedules.

timeline.title: Section 338 product list changes
timeline.detail: Rock salt and cement come off the tariff list; ATVs and more dairy products are added.

timeline.title: Alcohol and dairy bans take effect
timeline.detail: Certain Canadian alcohol and dairy products are barred from the US market.

timeline.title: USTR opens the 2027 USMCA review
timeline.detail: Written comments and hearing requests are due 12 January 2027.

timeline.title: Mexico pledges to buy more American goods
timeline.detail: It aims to secure a bilateral deal with Washington. Its goods surplus with the US from January to August rose 51% on a year earlier, to over $280bn.

timeline.title: Alberta votes to stay in Canada
timeline.detail: About 77% of voters rejected starting a path to independence, according to unofficial results.

timeline.title: Lawsuit against Section 338 duties reported
timeline.detail: A new lawsuit challenging the Section 338 tariffs on Canadian goods was reported on 20 October.

causes.name: Dairy and supply management
causes.detail: Canada's supply-managed dairy sector has long been a US grievance. The US cited dairy quota rules as a Section 338 ground and wants wider dairy access in the USMCA review.

causes.name: Canada's 2025 countermeasures
causes.detail: The US cited Canada's 25% surtax on US-made vehicles and provincial bans on US alcohol sales since March 2025 as grounds for Section 338.

causes.name: Trade-deficit politics
causes.detail: Washington treats bilateral deficits as a target, using tariffs as leverage.

causes.name: Collapse of trade talks
causes.detail: Talks broke down on 21 August, and the 50% Section 338 duties proclaimed on 20 July took effect the next day on about $20bn of Canadian goods.

causes.name: Non-extension of USMCA
causes.detail: The US refusal on 1 July to confirm a 16-year extension raised the stakes of the talks.

causes.name: Canadian retaliation
causes.detail: Dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs from 8 September prompted a sharper US response.

causes.name: Escalation from duties to bans
causes.detail: Five proclamations on 8 September turned the duties on certain alcohol and dairy products into bans and ordered Canadian-origin products off GSA schedules.

causes.name: Broad legal reach
causes.detail: Section 338 duties apply regardless of USMCA origin, and the White House says they apply in addition to Section 232 tariffs.

stakeholders.name: Donald Trump
stakeholders.wants: Concessions on dairy, autos and the deficit, and a campaign-season show of strength
stakeholders.leverage: Tariffs and bans by proclamation; market size; the USMCA review
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep the measures in place and use them as leverage in the yearly review

stakeholders.name: Mark Carney
stakeholders.wants: Protect Canadian producers, hold national unity and keep retaliation proportionate
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold dollar-for-dollar retaliation while courting the EU and other partners

stakeholders.name: Canadian provinces and producers
stakeholders.role: Dairy, wine, spirits, furniture and clothing sectors
stakeholders.leverage: Political pull on Ottawa; provincial liquor boards
stakeholders.likelyMove: Lobby for support funds and redirect exports where possible

stakeholders.name: US importers, retailers and consumers
stakeholders.likelyMove: Reroute sourcing, pass costs on, and press Congress and courts

stakeholders.name: Mexico
stakeholders.role: USMCA partner seeking a bilateral deal
stakeholders.wants: Secure access to the US market
stakeholders.leverage: Pledge to buy more American goods
stakeholders.likelyMove: Pursue a separate deal while avoiding Canada's fate

stakeholders.name: EU and other partners
stakeholders.leverage: Market access conditions such as CBAM and EUDR
stakeholders.likelyMove: Welcome Canadian overtures, with compliance conditions attached

sectors.why: US ban on certain dairy products plus Canadian counter-tariffs on US dairy.
The US ban on certain alcohol products removes a major export outlet.
A 50% tariff applies regardless of USMCA origin.

sectors.sector: US steel, appliances and farm equipment
sectors.why: Canada's counter-tariffs raise their prices in Canada.
More paperwork and rerouting, but lower volumes on some lanes.
Higher costs for Canadian furniture, cheese and other covered goods.

dailyLife.item: Cheese and dairy in the US
dailyLife.effect: Prices may rise as some Canadian supply is banned and domestic suppliers face less competition.

dailyLife.item: Canadian wine and spirits in US shops
dailyLife.effect: Banned products are expected to disappear from shelves while the ban lasts.
Canada's counter-tariffs on US appliances are likely to raise shelf prices.
The 50% duties on Canadian furniture are likely to feed into US home furnishing and renovation costs.
Canadian counter-tariffs raise the cost of US-made equipment for farmers.

scenarios.name: Prolonged standoff
scenarios.looksLike: Bans and counter-tariffs stay in place through the USMCA yearly review; talks are intermittent and fruitless.
signposts: No formal talks scheduled after 3 November
Both sides repeat their positions in the 12 January comments
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Canada diversifies slowly and US prices stay elevated; USMCA uncertainty lingers.

scenarios.name: Partial de-escalation
scenarios.looksLike: The bans are lifted back to tariffs or quotas, with Canada softening dairy terms and removing some counter-tariffs.
signposts: Canada offers movement on dairy access
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Relief for producers; the review continues with a smaller threat of collapse.

scenarios.name: Further escalation
scenarios.looksLike: New sectors added to the ban list or higher duties; Canada widens its counter-tariffs.
signposts: Canada extends retaliation to energy or autos
US treats USMCA withdrawal as a live option
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Broader price rises and supply-chain redesign across North America.

scenarios.name: Legal or political reset
scenarios.looksLike: A court ruling or post-midterm political shift undoes the Section 338 measures.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Return to the pre-August baseline, though with continuing 232 tariffs.

predictions.text: The bans on Canadian dairy and alcohol will still be in force on 31 December 2026 (probability 80%).
Canada will not remove its counter-tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances and farm equipment before the 3 November US midterms (probability 85%).
The US and Canada will announce a formal framework or ministerial talks aimed at lifting the bans (probability 30%).
Mexico will announce a bilateral trade arrangement with the US before Canada reaches any deal (probability 45%).
A US court will rule on a challenge to the Section 338 duties (probability 35%).

actions: Map which products fall under Section 338, which under Section 232, and which under Canada's counter-tariffs.
Do not rely on USMCA origin to avoid the 50% duties; check each line.
Add tariff-change and force-majeure clauses to contracts touching US-Canada flows.
Check whether any Canadian goods in your federal catalogue are affected by the GSA order.
Explore alternate suppliers or markets, including EU markets that need CBAM and EUDR compliance.
Treat the US-Canada dispute as political risk that is linked to the USMCA review and the midterms.
Watch Canadian agricultural, drinks and furniture exporters for earnings hits.
Watch US appliance and steel makers exposed to Canadian retaliation.
Expect higher prices for cheese, furniture and other covered Canadian goods in the US.
In Canada, expect US goods covered by counter-tariffs to cost more.
Avoid stockpiling beyond normal needs; the bans are not a supply emergency.
Separate the Section 338 legal question from the USMCA review so that one does not block the other.
Offer targeted support to affected producers rather than broad subsidies.
Coordinate with Mexico to keep the three-way review from fragmenting.

analogues.whatFollowed: Canada retaliated, trade shrank sharply, and the episode became the standard warning against tariff spirals. Section 338 comes from the same Tariff Act.

analogues.event: US steel and aluminium tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs
analogues.whatFollowed: Canada imposed counter-tariffs in 2018 and lifted them in 2019 as part of the deal that cleared the way for USMCA ratification.
Repeated tariffs and settlements; the disputes went on for decades without full resolution.

analogues.event: US-Canada tariff clash and provincial boycotts of US alcohol
analogues.whatFollowed: Provinces pulled US alcohol from shelves and counter-tariffs were imposed; to our knowledge, the pressure did not produce a lasting settlement.

evidence.method: This dossier was drafted from two sources (a White House fact sheet and an Al Jazeera report), their headlines and a short event summary. On 20 October an AI fact-checker checked each factual claim against those sources and against law-firm analyses of the Section 338 proclamations, trade press and news reports, which are added to the source list. Claims that could not be confirmed were removed or reworded, and price effects are presented as judgement. The historical analogues are general knowledge. All probabilities, scenarios and predictions are estimates, and no price or trade-volume series was available, so no chart is included.
